analysis.one_liner: Extends federal ethanol tax credits for five years and keeps the tariff on imported ethanol in place.
analysis.headline: Despite 46 bipartisan cosponsors, the ethanol credit and tariff extension never got a committee vote and died when the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would extend through 2015 the main federal tax credits for ethanol, including the credit paid to companies that blend ethanol into gasoline, plus the tax credit for cellulosic biofuel. It would also extend the special tariff on imported ethanol until 2016, keeping cheaper foreign ethanol out [S2][S3]. The bill never received a vote: it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and then to its Trade Subcommittee, and it died there when the Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Corn ethanol producers, who would keep the credits that support demand and prices for their product through 2015 [S2][S3]. Fuel blenders, who collect the 45-cent-per-gallon blending credit from the Treasury [S2][S3]. Corn growers and rural communities in ethanol-producing states, whose corn demand and jobs the credits and tariff help sustain.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Corn ethanol producers and fuel blenders

how_it_helps.text: Extends the income and excise tax credits for alcohol used as fuel, and the tax credit for cellulosic biofuel producers, through the end of 2015, rather than letting them expire at the end of 2010 [S2][S3].
Extends the reduced credit for ethanol blenders through 2015, continuing the per-gallon payment that blenders claim against their tax bills [S2][S3].
Extends the additional tariff on fuel ethanol until 2016, which shields domestic corn ethanol from cheaper imported ethanol, mainly Brazilian sugarcane ethanol [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, who would fund roughly five more years of ethanol tax credits — the main blenders credit was costing the Treasury several billion dollars a year at the time. Motor-fuel consumers also pay through the tariff, which keeps lower-priced imported ethanol off the market.

drawbacks.text: Extending the credits through 2015 would continue a multi-billion-dollar-a-year drain on the Treasury for a mature industry, with no reforms or phase-down attached [S2][S3].

The tariff extension keeps cheaper imported ethanol out of the market until 2016, raising fuel costs and blocking Brazilian sugarcane ethanol, which delivers larger greenhouse-gas reductions per gallon than corn ethanol — so the bill undercuts its own environmental rationale [S2][S3].

The blenders credit flows to large fuel-blending companies regardless of whether the ethanol market needs support, so much of the subsidy is captured by established firms rather than new investment [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real but concentrated: ethanol plants, corn growers, and blenders in a handful of Midwest states gain guaranteed support and tariff protection. The costs are diffuse but large: five more years of tax credits paid by all federal taxpayers, plus higher fuel input costs from keeping out cheaper imports. Corn ethanol's climate benefit is weak compared to other renewables and to sugarcane ethanol, so extending the whole package unchanged is a poor deal for the general public even by the standards of energy subsidy bills.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Ways and Means Committee and then its Trade Subcommittee and never got a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Earl Pomeroy of North Dakota introduced the bill on March 25, 2010, joined by 29 original cosponsors from both parties, concentrated in Corn Belt and Plains states [S1][S3].
It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the same day, and on April 9, 2010 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Trade [S5].
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed, and the bill died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S1][S5].

Congress did briefly extend the ethanol credits for 2011 in a separate year-end tax bill, but the credits and the import tariff were then allowed to lapse at the end of 2011 — so the five-year lock-in this bill sought never happened (widely reported).

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Taxpayers and fuel consumers came out ahead, because the five-year extension of the credits and the import tariff never advanced. The ethanol industry and Corn Belt members lost their push for a long-term lock-in, and the blenders credit and tariff lapsed at the end of 2011.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers; ethanol industry lost its extension

for.name: Earl Pomeroy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited the original bipartisan cosponsor group.

for.name: Ethanol and corn-grower interests
for.what_they_did: Backed extension of the ethanol credits and import tariff, which protect their markets and revenue.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill; it was referred to the Trade Subcommittee on April 9, 2010 and never advanced to a markup or floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan and regional rather than partisan: 26 of 253 House Democrats and 20 of 178 House Republicans cosponsored, mostly from Corn Belt states, and no one voted against it because it never reached a vote.

industries.note: The extended credits prop up demand and prices for corn ethanol through 2015, and the extended tariff blocks cheaper Brazilian sugarcane ethanol until 2016. The industry's gain comes directly from taxpayer-funded credits and from higher fuel input costs for consumers.

The blending credit is paid to the companies that mix ethanol into gasoline, so the extension is a direct Treasury payment to blenders for five more years. Their interest in the bill runs against taxpayers' interest.

Guaranteed ethanol demand and tariff protection support corn prices and rural incomes, including family farms in ethanol states. But that income is sustained by subsidies and tariffs paid for by all taxpayers and fuel buyers, and the renewable fuel mandate already guarantees much of their market.

The extended tariff keeps their lower-cost, lower-carbon ethanol out of the U.S. market until 2016. Their interest in open access to the U.S. market runs alongside consumers' interest in cheaper fuel.
